Let \(\delta=3\). More generally, put
\[
\Delta_0=1,\qquad \Delta_1=\delta,\qquad \Delta_{r+1}=\delta\Delta_r-\Delta_{r-1}.
\]

For noncrossing matchings, use the usual Dyck-path encoding: scanning the \(12\) points in order, write \(U\) at the left endpoint of an arc and \(D\) at the right endpoint. Thus \(\mathcal M\) is identified with Dyck paths of semilength \(6\).

A standard Gram-Schmidt elimination on these Dyck paths gives the determinant of the meander Gram matrix as
\[
\det A=\prod_{\gamma}\prod_{\substack{\text{down steps of }\gamma\\ h\to h-1}}
\frac{\Delta_h}{\Delta_{h-1}},
\]
where \(\gamma\) runs over all Dyck paths of semilength \(6\), and \(h\) is the height before the down step.

Briefly, the reason is that when a new closing arc lowers height \(h\to h-1\), the Schur-complement pivot is
\[
\delta-\frac{\Delta_{h-2}}{\Delta_{h-1}}
=\frac{\delta\Delta_{h-1}-\Delta_{h-2}}{\Delta_{h-1}}
=\frac{\Delta_h}{\Delta_{h-1}},
\]
with the case \(h=1\) giving \(\Delta_1/\Delta_0=\delta\). Multiplying these pivots over the Dyck-path basis gives the formula above.

Let \(m_h\) be the total number of down steps from height \(h\) among all Dyck paths of semilength \(6\). Counting prefixes and suffixes gives
\[
(m_1,m_2,m_3,m_4,m_5,m_6)=(297,275,154,54,11,1).
\]
Therefore the exponent of \(\Delta_h\) is \(m_h-m_{h+1}\), with \(m_7=0\), so
\[
(e_1,e_2,e_3,e_4,e_5,e_6)
=(22,121,100,43,10,1).
\]

Now evaluate at \(\delta=3\):
\[
\Delta_1=3,\quad
\Delta_2=8,\quad
\Delta_3=21,\quad
\Delta_4=55,\quad
\Delta_5=144,\quad
\Delta_6=377.
\]
Hence
\[
\det A
=3^{22}8^{121}21^{100}55^{43}144^{10}377.
\]
Factoring,
\[
\det A
=2^{403}3^{142}5^{43}7^{100}11^{43}\cdot 13\cdot 29.
\]

\[
\boxed{2^{403}3^{142}5^{43}7^{100}11^{43}\cdot13\cdot29}
\]
